title: When the Corrector Is the Noise: LLM OCR Repair After ICDAR 2026

body:
Historical OCR has been a quiet bottleneck for decades. Every quantitative claim a historian or sociologist makes about a newspaper archive — the frequency of a phrase, the co-occurrence of two entities, the sentiment trajectory of a column — is a composition of two layers: the archive's digitised image, and the OCR model that turns it into text. When the OCR is good, these layers vanish from the analysis. When it is bad, they colour everything downstream. The first HIPE-OCRepair competition at ICDAR 2026 (Ehrmann, Boros, Opitz, Michail, Wagner and Clematide, arXiv:2607.08143) was the first large, multi-dataset, multi-language benchmark to ask whether modern LLM-based correctors can collapse that distance. The headline answer is "mostly yes, on noisy text." The quieter finding is sharper: on text that was already clean, several systems made it measurably worse. That inversion is the subject of this post.

## Why this matters now

Several things changed at once. OCR engines are now competitive on nineteenth- and twentieth-century printed text, so raw character error rates on well-preserved sources are already low. LLMs are being drafted in as general-purpose post-correctors on top of that pipeline, and their use is spreading from research code to production ingest pipelines in cultural institutions and retrieval indexes over newspaper archives. The ICDAR 2026 release — a package of `icdar2017`, `impresso-snippets`, `impresso-nzz`, `overproof`, and `dta19` at three noise levels, across English, French and German, 17th through 20th century — and its scorer were the first machinery that lets you check the second layer without the first. The gold transcription is held out, the primary metric is reported with 10,000-resample bootstrap intervals, and four teams submitted systems spanning zero-shot prompting to continued pre-training. The competition replaced the vibe-based claim "LLMs are better at this" with a number.

## What MER actually measures, and what it hides

Call the hypothesis $h$ and the gold $g$. The classic character error rate is $\text{CER} = (S + D + I) / N$, where $S$, $D$, $I$ are the substitutions, deletions and insertions on the shortest edit path and $N$ is the length of $g$. CER is unbounded above: a corrector that hallucinates text longer than the gold can score $\text{CER} > 1$. The Match Error Rate rescales this by putting insertions in the denominator as well,

$$ \text{MER} \;=\; \frac{S + D + I}{H + S + D + I}, $$

where $H$ is hits and the denominator is the total alignment length. MER lives in $[0, 1]$ and treats hallucinated characters symmetrically with missed ones. Normalised — lowercase, letter-plus-digit tokens, accent-sensitive, punctuation stripped — it is the cMER the HIPE-OCRepair scorer reports. Micro-averaged (`cmer_micro`) across transcription units in a dataset, longer units count more; macro-averaging gives each unit equal weight.

cMER has two useful properties and one danger. First, it is smooth under layout noise: the scorer removes soft hyphens at line breaks and converts remaining line breaks to spaces, so systems are not penalised for reflowing. Second, it is numerically stable on noisy inputs, because the insertion penalty is bounded. The danger is the usual averaging danger: a corrector that improves half the documents by 5% and degrades the other half by 5% has the same cMER as a corrector that touches nothing. The ICDAR scorer separates these by also reporting a *preference score*: per document, compare the corrected output and the raw OCR against the gold, award $+1$ if the correction wins, $0$ if tied, $-1$ if it loses, and macro-average across documents. A score near $+1$ says the corrector is almost always a net improvement; a score near $0$ says it is a coin flip. On the French track, BnF-Mistral's best run landed at cMER $\approx 0.0042$ and preference $\approx 0.93$. A sister run reported a slightly better preference ($\approx 0.95$) but a worse cMER ($\approx 0.0068$), because it was more willing to edit and more often slightly wrong when it did. The two numbers reward different behaviours, and the results table is more informative than either alone.

## The over-correction regime

Over-correction is what happens when a corrector's prior over "clean modern text" is stronger than its willingness to leave the input alone. Several things fall under that name. The mildest is silent style normalisation: a model trained on contemporary text modernises an archaic spelling the OCR was already reading correctly. A sharper version is period hallucination in the other direction, which Levchenko (LM4DH 2025, arXiv:2510.06743) names *over-historicisation*. Her 12-model study on 18th-century Russian Civil-font texts found that Gemini and Qwen variants beat classical OCR on raw error, but inserted archaic characters from the wrong historical period more often than the OCR itself did. To isolate these failures, she introduces two metrics tailored to diplomatic transcription: Historical Character Preservation Rate (HCPR), the fraction of period-specific characters (the pre-reform *і/ї*, *ѣ*, *ъ*) that survive the model's pass, and Archaic Insertion Rate (AIR), the rate at which the model inserts obsolete characters where the gold has modern ones. Standard CER and MER are blind to both: the substitution penalty is the same whether the model guessed the wrong modern letter or the wrong century's letter.

The HIPE-OCRepair paper sees over-correction from the other side. On the cleanest German subset (`dta19` level 0), several systems turned a near-zero baseline into something slightly worse, because any edit was more likely to introduce an error than to fix one. The lower the raw OCR error, the thinner the margin for useful editing, and the louder the model's prior gets heard. Under either framing the mechanism is the same: the corrector is being asked to do inference under a loss that penalises *difference from gold* and rewards *agreement with its prior*, and when the two conflict, the prior wins.

## A concrete anchor

The two scores are easy enough to compute on a single document to see what they do. Suppose you have a gold string $g$, a raw OCR hypothesis $h_{\text{raw}}$, and a corrected hypothesis $h_{\text{fix}}$. A toy version of the HIPE-OCRepair scorer, on a single unit:

```python
import re, unicodedata
from jiwer import compute_measures

def normalise(s):
    s = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s).lower()
    s = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", " ", s)
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()

def mer(gold, hyp):
    g, h = normalise(gold), normalise(hyp)
    return compute_measures(list(g), list(h))["mer"]

def score_unit(gold, raw, fix):
    m_raw, m_fix = mer(gold, raw), mer(gold, fix)
    if m_fix < m_raw:   pref = +1
    elif m_fix > m_raw: pref = -1
    else:               pref = 0
    return m_raw, m_fix, pref

gold = "the quick brown fox"
raw  = "th3 quick brown fox"     # one noisy character
fix1 = "the quick brown fox"     # clean fix
fix2 = "the quick brown fox."    # trailing punctuation only
fix3 = "the fast brown fox"      # introduced a content change

for h in (fix1, fix2, fix3):
    print(score_unit(gold, raw, h))
```

Three behaviours fall out. The first is the regime where a corrector should operate: visible error in, clean fix out, preference $+1$. The second shows why punctuation-insensitive normalisation matters — a trailing period does not count against the system. The third is the over-correction signature: the input was fine except for a numeral, and the "fix" rewrote a content word, pushing cMER up and preference to $-1$. Aggregated over a dataset, that third pattern is what the preference score surfaces and cMER alone can hide.

## What this implies in practice

If you are using an LLM to post-correct historical OCR, three things follow. First, do not run correction unconditionally. Condition on a cheap estimate of the raw error — the `no_edits` and `random_edits` baseline rows in the HIPE-OCRepair release are useful anchors — and route only the noisy fraction to the LLM; the clean fraction is already better than any corrector has made it. In the competition, LLM systems dominated on moderate-to-high-noise tracks; on `dta19` level 0, the raw OCR is a strong baseline most LLMs struggled to beat. Second, report both cMER and preference score, and look at the second before you believe the first: a 0.1 improvement in cMER with a preference score near $0.4$ means you have improved the long documents and silently degraded the short ones. Third, if you are working on diplomatic transcription for scholarly use, standard character-level scores do not see the errors that matter. Measure HCPR and AIR, or their domain analogues, and treat the LLM's prior as a hyperparameter to be checked, not a given.

## Limits and open questions

The ICDAR 2026 scoring is retrieval-oriented by design: lowercase, punctuation stripped, accents kept. That matches many downstream text-mining uses — search indexes, topic models, named-entity pipelines — but not editorial ones. A scholarly edition cares about punctuation and case; a measurement by normalised cMER can look good while hiding exactly the errors an editor would reject. A diplomatic-transcription companion metric is a natural next step and is not yet standardised. More broadly, there is no agreed metric for over-correction itself. Levchenko's HCPR and AIR are early and language-specific, and the HIPE-OCRepair documentation treats over-correction as a diagnosis rather than a quantity. A conservative candidate would be preference score conditioned on raw-OCR noise bin, because that directly measures "did I make easy documents worse?"; a more ambitious one would separate stylistic normalisation (modernisation) from substantive hallucination (content drift).

The competition's team pool was small — four — and the data release is biased toward Western European printed sources. Results on scripts with unstable segmentation (Arabic, Devanagari), on handwritten rather than printed material, and on languages whose prior is weak because the pre-training mix is thin, are not covered. Work from adjacent corners is already pushing back. Do, Tran, Vo and Kim (arXiv:2410.13305, AAAI 2025 AISI track) show that reference-grounded post-correction — giving the LLM an aligned ebook of the same work as evidence — closes much of the diacritic gap for classical Vietnamese. Hoenen's small-scale 2026 study on 18th-century handwritten Church Slavonic Valamo-monastery manuscripts (arXiv:2604.11724) finds that LLMs help only once agentic correction loops and references are added; generic "thinking" or "web-search" modes in off-the-shelf models frequently performed worse than direct post-correction prompts. Both results argue that the positive HIPE-OCRepair verdict on printed European newspapers is not immediately a general-script claim, and that where the model's prior is thin, the corrector needs extra evidence rather than more parameters.

## Further reading

- Maud Ehrmann, Emanuela Boros, Juri Opitz, Andrianos Michail, Florian Wagner, Simon Clematide, *ICDAR 2026 HIPE-OCRepair Competition on LLM-Assisted OCR Post-Correction for Historical Documents*, arXiv:2607.08143. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08143>. The primary benchmark: datasets, scorer and leaderboard released; the source for cMER and preference-score numbers used above.
- Maria Levchenko, *Evaluating LLMs for Historical Document OCR: A Methodological Framework for Digital Humanities*, LM4DH 2025, arXiv:2510.06743. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06743>. The paper that names the over-historicisation failure and defines HCPR and AIR, with a 12-model study on 18th-century Russian Civil-font texts and contamination controls.
- HIPE-OCRepair scorer repository. <https://github.com/hipe-eval/HIPE-OCRepair-scorer>. The MER / cMER / preference-score implementation with bootstrap intervals and dataset-stratified reporting; the reference module for reproducible scoring.
- HIPE-OCRepair-2026 data repository. <https://github.com/hipe-eval/HIPE-OCRepair-2026-data>. The dataset release, participation guidelines, scoring protocol and the `no_edits`/`random_edits` baselines; useful not only to reproduce the competition but as a template for similar benchmarks in other languages.
- Thao Do, Dinh Phu Tran, An Vo, Daeyoung Kim, *Reference-Based Post-OCR Processing with LLM for Precise Diacritic Text in Historical Document Recognition*, arXiv:2410.13305 (AAAI 2025 AISI). <https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13305>. Reference-grounded alternative: give the corrector an aligned ebook of the same work and over-correction drops sharply.
- Armin Hoenen, *The Devil is in the Details — From OCR for Old Church Slavonic to Purely Visual Stemma Reconstruction*, arXiv:2604.11724. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11724>. A small-scale but careful comparison on three Valamo-monastery handwritten manuscripts; agentic correction loops help, naive correction does not.
